name: unit-model-compare
notes:
Flip 'unlimited workers' live: off vs on, identical sine load (period 200s) and identical knobs otherwise. Measured (seed 1, same run length): off, the worker pool itself is the bottleneck per instance — bounded at ceil(cores*(cpuTimeMs+ioWaitMs)/cpuTimeMs) = ceil(2*(30+120)/30) = 10 worker slots, plus 8 queue slots, so it rejects past capacity. Errors settle at ~1.7%, latency stays bounded (max 262ms, mean 155ms across the run). On, workers never reject, but the CPU pool (2 cores) still saturates for real: errors drop to 0% — nothing gets rejected -- but latency balloons: mean 1383ms (9x worse), max 29.9 SECONDS as queued requests pile up waiting for a core. Peak instance count is identical either way (16 instances in the cluster), because the controller's target-utilization math doesn't change.

Two things are true at once here, both worth saying out loud:

1. The controller isn't blind. `cpu` here is now an honest, measured busy fraction of the real CPU pool -- not the old cpuReport approximation of event-loop utilization. It rises with real load and drives the same scale-out decisions in both variants, which is why peak instances match (16 either way). The metric was never the thing that changed; it's what happens to a request that arrives once the metric has already said 'more'.

2. Off, admission control happens once, at the worker pool: a request that can't get a worker (and doesn't fit in the 8-slot queue) is rejected immediately and cleanly, so total in-flight work -- and worst-case latency for anything that IS admitted -- stays bounded. On, there's no admission control left to trip: every request is accepted and simply queues for a core, so the failure mode moves from a fast, honest rejection to a silent, unbounded wait. Zero errors looks like success on a dashboard that only tracks error rate -- it isn't.
